text: When you type a web address, your browser has to turn it into an IP address, and DNS resolution does that. It starts with a check of your browser cache, which holds recently visited sites. If the answer isn't there, the request goes to a recursive resolver. The resolver asks a root server where to look and gets pointed to the right top-level domain server, such as .com or .org. That server leads it to the authoritative server, which holds the exact address for the site. Once the resolver has the answer, it hands it back to your device and stores it for a while. The TTL, or time to live, controls how long that lasts, and it's typically about 300 seconds. That makes the next visit faster. All of this happens in a fraction of a second.
